text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed sharply higher on the back of a fund-led rally in New York raw futures. By the close August was up $4.30 at $315.20 per tonne, while October added $2.30 to close at $307.20 per tonne. Raw sugar futures in New York closed sharply higher in a heavily traded session with July holding support at 11.20 cents/lb despite steady trade selling throughout the day. May added 26 points to close at 11.53 cents/lb, while July closed 12 points higher at 11.24 cents/lb. The outer months gained between 8 and 10 points. Physical demand continues to be slack.

Cuba dominated the thin amount of new quoted business on London's sugar freight market on April 23 with the Black Sea as destination. Market talk suggested Cuba could be retaining some of its raw sugar as physical prices firm before Brazil returns as an exporter with its Center South crop. There seems to be no fundamental reason behind today's price rise and the market looks overbought. It is expected that Brazil will publish its crop plan for 1997/98 at the end of April. The government has given top priority to alcohol production to phase out imports.

RUSSIA - While Russia's 1997 spring sowing campaign is ahead of 1996's depressed levels, with 2.75 million ha planted by April 21, up 6 to 7 percent on a year ago, sugar beet sowings are lagging behind. According to official sources the area sown by April 21 reached 148,000 ha, one percent down from the same period last year.

BRAZIL - Industry representatives and government officials will meet today to hammer out the 1997/98 (May/April) crop plan which is slated for publication on April 30. The government's priority this year is to produce enough alcohol to eliminate the need for imports and despite expectations of a higher cane crop, sugar production will only be marginally higher than last year, Pedro Cabral, head of the sugar and alcohol department at the Industry Ministry said.

In previous years the crop plan detailed production of sugar and alcohol as well as export allowances per factory. But while producers in the largest growing state of Sao Paulo accept a plan for alcohol and for the internal sugar market, they do reject the idea of fixed exports but would rather see producers to decide for themselves which volumes to ship. According to some industry estimates, the total surplus amount in 1997/98 could reach around 6 million tonnes of which 4.4 million in the Center South and 1.6 million in the North/Northeast.

However, others expect alcohol production to rise to such an extent that even exports could become a possibility. They argue that the USA could emerge as a lucrative export market after US soybean stocks hit historical lows prompting compound feeders to use more maize in their formulas. This move together with expected tightness in other grains has driven up maize quotations in recent weeks thus boosting the price of ethanol. If this expectation turns out to be correct sugar export estimates of around 6 million tonnes would clearly be unattainable even if cane output should rise to 310 million tonnes as forecast.

FRANCE - Sugar imports in January 1997 amounted to 24,094 tonnes, raw value, sharply down from last year's 60,596 tonnes. This brought cumulative imports in the first four months of 1996/97 (October/January) up to 157,579 tonnes against 183,767 tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 476,587 tonnes compared to 364,140 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of origin in October/January 1996/97 were Reunion with 40,501 tonnes raws against 64,697 tonnes and Swaziland with 25,963 tonnes, down from 41,874 tonnes. Sugar exports in January 1997 were also down at 141,218 tonnes compared to 210,609 tonnes in January 1996.

This brought cumulative exports in October/January 1996/97 up to 1.103 million tonnes against 1.177 million tonnes in 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 reached 2.896 million tonnes against 3.067 million tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of destination in October/January 1996/97 were Belgium-Luxembourg with 272,293 tonnes whites against 321,434 tonnes, Algeria with 125,773 tonnes, up from 42,273 tonnes and Saudi Arabia with 77,759 tonnes compared to 59,241 tonnes.

The European Union awarded 73,500 tonnes of white sugar at a maximum refund of ECU 43.542 per 100 kg at its weekly tender on April 23. Cumulative awards so far made under the 1996/97 series of tenders for the period up to April 23 reached 1,870,550 tonnes, which compares to 2,006,298 tonnes last year.
